Show HN: Foldocs, turn a shared Google Drive or Nextcloud folder into a website
items.summary: I built something for someone who needed a website, but didn't want to be exposed to yet another complicated CMS like WordPress. They already use Google Docs, so I built Foldocs for them to publish and maintain a simple website. Foldocs creates static HTML pages out of a (shared) fol der of doc uments in Google Drive (or Nextcloud!): (sub)folders become (sub)sections on the site, and documents inside them become pages. Does it work? Proof is to be found in the pudding: Foldocs.com, the site that explains Foldocs, is itself a Foldocs site! The underlying Google Drive is here: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1ZRYhiIGfSeIcA_gjRVgT... . Foldocs is an open source (AGPL 3.0) Python engine anyone can run. It currently supports three themes, dark mode, and an RSS feed. You can also try it out by creating a preview on https://try.foldocs.com . Paste a shared folder link, and see a preview (kept for 7 days, limited in files / size, and only syncs manually). Previews are running on a separate domain and a throwaway VPS, since hosting strangers' content on the internet is... scary. Curious to hear what you think of the concept, learn what breaks (but don't try too hard please), what you run into, and/or what is missing!

items.title: Show HN: Markdown is 40× more token-efficient with SQLite
items.summary: Hi HN, I'm Richard, founder of Native. I'm working on open-source context ownership, to stop AI centralisation: https://github.com/withnative/native My first focus has been making Markdown vaults powerful enough so that teams can self-host all of their context (messaging, docs and projects), without it being externally fragmented or rate-limited. I'm sharing some early results: Markdown vaults can be 40× more efficient with SQLite! https://www.withnative.ai/research-and-posts/markdown-contex... Here's some of the main ideas: - SQLite or Markdown folders, you pick. You can project the same authoritative event log into either form; more projection formats will follow (e.g. maybe neo4j; we do use a graph structure). - Empirically: SQLite is better for agents! On a 120 trial evaluation for 11,000 records, agents use 40× fewer tokens with SQLite vs Markdown, per correct answer. - Everything is a file or SQLite row. Messages, documents and projects: all can be modelled in your vault. You get local-first collaboration with teammates, synced to a cloud of your choice. - You can render your vault with arbitrary UI. Your WhatsApp-like UI speaks to your teammate's Slack-like UI; both are just views over the same database. A few things I've learned building this: - Agents do pretty well even without SQL if you give them strongly typed Markdown frontmatter. This was one arm of the trial I ran. I didn't have any clear expectations, but it was cool to watch: agents ended up writing Python scripts to do SQL-like queries. - Cumulatively, cached input tokens can get expensive. I feel silly in hindsight here. I'd gotten used to letting my sessions run long, "It's all cached so it's very cheap". But when I looked at my results here, over 2/3 of the token bill on long sessions was cached input... - "Markdown vaults don't scale as well as databases" isn't as self-evident as I think. This is why I decided to benchmark it... I've had some very blank stares when I try to explain how Markdown files might break at true agent-scale volume. Unfortunately, the dataset is private, because it's two months of my own work. I am considering open-sourcing it even so, but there is definitely some embarrassing stuff in there. TBD... I know that independent result verification matters! The core engine that I evaluated is open-source, with more to be released soon: https://github.com/withnative/native If you're interested in trying connected context on an open engine, you can get updates from our website or email me directly: richard@withnative.ai https://www.withnative.ai/
